en: The Sutra on the Buddha’s Teaching on the Contemplation of the Inner Body,
translated by an unknown author and included in the Later Han Catalogue.
(1) Unify the mind and listen entirely to the beautiful words of instruction.
Listen now to that sūtra from which the Buddha attained the Way:
That emptiness is not annihilation; all conditioned formations are impermanent.
Yet, because formations do not utterly perish, the Buddha has preached this sūtra.
Matters profound and subtle are difficult to perceive; they are not the words of Zhang Yuan.
Only one who penetrates them can expound upon them, and for this reason he is the Teacher.
Following the origin to preserve the source, there is the accumulation of the cultivation of the Dharma.
Abandoning through wisdom—this is what the Superior One has taught.
Whatever exists arises from causes and conditions; all conditioned formations (saṃskāra) are non-existent.
Furthermore, there is the removal of past lives; one does not perceive those various formations.
Just as one who wishes to manifest their body, As taught by the Kinsman of the Sun (the Buddha),
Whose great calamities and afflictions are innumerable, All of which flow back toward the body;
Thus have I edited according to the original text, These essential words that have been expounded.
The five-character verses are magnificent and ornate, clarifying vows to provide encouragement.
With the full complement of poetic diction, the even-numbered syllables are harmoniously prepared;
like flowers and fruits mingled together, all listen to the instructions of both self and others.
The body is neither a person nor a life-force; it is not a great man nor a noble.
Whether as a physical entity or as something beautiful, such things do not exist at all.
For the body is created through conditions, and that which exists is subject to decay and death.
All that lacks strength must take refuge [in the truth], for like a bubble it crumbles under the tread;
what lacks strength is impermanent, and what is impermanent is without pleasure;
what is impermanent is also suffering, and that which is not the body is not the self.
The body is impermanent and suffering; it should not be regarded as one's self.
If the substance of the body were identical with the self, then the body would never cease to exist;
yet since the body has no such substantiality, it both comes into being and perishes.
The wise, by means of the beginning and the end, see that how could those [dharmas] already possess a self-nature?
If they are without a master, they cannot be independent.
Since there is such calculation and analysis, how could those entities belong to a self?
This physical body is empty; the self is unreal and conditioned.
It exists as a result of causes and conditions; it does not perish with the body nor is it created by the mind.
It is not created by the bodies of others, nor is it created by one's own body.
The body has no creator, nor is there anything that the body does not create.
Because the body has no creator, one attains the Truth through that.
Coming from previous lives, the body was likewise not created by a god.
This city is not conjured by a deity; it is not without activity, nor is it without a basis.
It does not exist of itself without a cause; this body has its origins—it arises from conditions and consists of constituent things.
Gradually there arises the existence of birth; its root is both delusion and craving.
When the mind possesses the outflows of craving, it is both bound and fettered;
the two categories of formations constitute the outflows.
The world and its causes for sensation arise; because of them, this body exists, and through gradual stages, existence is brought about.
From the essence of foam, it gradually solidifies; from the feet, the two pairs [of limbs] are produced.
With two [joints] it turns and thickens; with sequence it possesses four bodies.
It is the fifth for the formation of the head; various bones accumulate, and through movement they are formed into function. The head consists of nine [bones], the skull being one.
The two cheekbones constitute two bones; the roots of the thirty-two teeth consist of thirty-two bones;
the teeth themselves consist of thirty-two bones.
The neck and the base of the ears, the nose and the upper palate, as well as the heart and the throat—these are [all distinct].
In total, there are eighty bones.
The throat also consists of four bones; the left arm and the right arm together comprise fifty bones.
If this left side has ribs, there should be thirteen;
likewise for this right side, there should also be thirteen ribs—thus making forty-eight in total.
The three sets of three are interconnected, and the two sets of two are interconnected;
the rest are not interconnected, for the body is held together by strength.
Like a bundle of reeds, it has no inherent strength; there are thirty-two vertebrae in the spine.
The buttocks and the waist make three; likewise,
the left thigh bone is twenty-five bones,
and the right thigh is also the same, being twenty-five bones.
There are four bones in the shoulders and thighs, totaling three hundred and twenty.
The Buddha severed the succession [of rebirth] on this day;
all those fragments were gathered together, and the various sense-faculties (*indriya*) served as the seams. Though it was not a wound, he wrapped it [in robes].
Smeared with flesh and blood, it is like a wooden mechanical device held together by threads,
or like a magician’s illusion.
Bound and fastened by sinews, the collection of bones is thus assembled.
Regarding this as a physical form,
no fool fails to become attached to it, yet the wise do not become attached.
The nine apertures are great sores, and its circumference is a constant leakage.
This body is like an impure, putrid place,
with its mouth and nostrils like hollows filled with various grains;
it contains various internal organs, as well as hair, fur, nails, and teeth.
Dust and also skin and leather, Bones and joints as well as marrow,
Ordinary sinews and vessels, The stomach, the heart, and also the spleen,
The large intestine and also the small intestine, The liver and the lungs as well as the kidneys.
Fat and excrement, tears and saliva as well as sweat,
nasal mucus, grease, and blood, cold-fever fat and urine,
the sinews and the membranes— all these cause one to sink down into that [realm].
Like an old ox smeared with mud, one does not realize it has become so.
Within and without the body, the bones are like a city wall, adorned with flesh and blood as its plaster; yet it is destroyed by its enemies.
Constantly, both within and without, hundreds upon hundreds of various beings desire its flesh;
likewise, external calamities and disasters all blame it for its many faults—
this body is but a rotting and decaying thing.
It is like an ancient city, attended to day and night;
though it crumbles, it crumbles again, like a pit or a deserted village;
where thieves always dwell together, seizing and deceiving those who approach.
The body is the lair of a venomous serpent; for the venomous serpent is most virulent.
It constantly dwells within the person, its poisonous and treacherous malice manifesting as anger and joy—a great poison that prevents harmony.
Always remaining harmonious and at peace, for when one is angry there is no reciprocity,
and in an instant one is again unsettled.
To harbor resentment brings fear, like a tiger roaming through a desolate marsh.
It is full of dread and many terrors;
all thoughts look up toward it as their support, yet it is a vessel for all suffering and the site of all agonizing events.
This body, as its master, undergoes these experiences, sinking into the nature of suffering.
The body is the abode of all diseases, subject to the laws of old age and death.
It increases attachment and craving;
it suffers from cold and heat, or from the disharmony of wind—thus, illness arises as if born anew.
The senses are ruined, and the swift thief of loss harms people;
old age and death oppress and afflict humanity, like a mass of snow meeting fire,
which quickly causes it to dissolve.
The many calamities and misfortunes of the body— all that I have expounded—
cannot yet be fully detailed.
This decaying body is unsubstantial, having been formed through a multitude of causes and conditions.
Taking the Great [Self] as one’s body.
In the *Buddha-spoken Sūtra on the Contemplation of the Internal Body*, Chapter Eleven on the Causes and Conditions, the Buddha said:

"The practitioner has eleven causes and conditions that, through cessation, the path, and restraint, prevent a person from falling into the evil realms. That which should not be recognized is called 'the myriad things'."
First is "great assembly," which refers to a multitude of people;
second is "eating much," which refers to various delicacies, as well as overeating;
third is "much activity," which refers to many karmic actions.
Fourth is excessive clamor, meaning excessive speech;
fifth is excessive sleep;
sixth is social gathering, meaning [excessive involvement] within meditative concentration.
Seventh is habitual practice, which refers to being preoccupied with many affairs;
eighth is attachment to the body;
ninth is frivolity, which refers to speech that is not in accordance with the Dharma.
The tenth is greed, meaning excessive desire;
the eleventh is not dwelling in a favorable place, meaning among evil people.
A practitioner of the Path should sever these eleven causal conditions to attain the Path swiftly.
"Thus [he spoke]."
